samples.prompt: Write a reflective narrative about revisiting a memory from your youth involving an unfinished or newly constructed building. Describe your philosophical impressions of the empty structure at the time and include a specific incident or action you took during your visit.
samples.generated:
There was one more thing I must see; the new house for the great
schoolmaster. It seemed strange that he had built it in advance, as if
he had already decided to be out of sight and mind. I walked up and down
the empty streets of the village with my thoughts all about it. I thought
of the old saying that no man could love his work until he had finished
it. I knew the true meaning of this. I had been there, standing at the
threshold of the great building and watching the sun setting upon the
great landscape like the setting of a portrait. But the work was
unfinished, like a picture by the old master who is still working on it,
and the man who made it is still living in it. As I walked down the
street again after this last look at the house, I came to a small door in
a little cottage which looked as if it might belong to the schoolmaster.
I knocked and a little man with a white beard opened the door.

“Good-day, sir,” he said, “I know you are the poet.”

“No,” I replied, “I am nobody but a <ORG>, but you have made me come
here, so let us talk about poetry and about the building.”

“I don't know much about poetry,” he said, “but I think you may find
what you want in the library;”

“Thank you,” I answered, “but I should rather like to read about the
building.”

But when we consider the great matter which has been the subject of this
little volume—that is, the matter of the real and true use of our
intellects—then it becomes obvious that we are not only talking about
the use of the intellect, but about the use of the eye, the use of the
hand, the use of the foot, or the use of the whole body; for, as I have
said before, what is meant by the use of the intellect is nothing more
nor less than the power of using things in connection with it. Now,
there is an easy and natural way of doing this, which I will compare
with the process of using a hammer. If I wish to use a hammer, I must
first be aware that there is a nail that needs driving into wood; and I
must therefore first be aware of the nail. There is no need for me to
discover the nail; I can discover the nail because I know that nails
need driving into wood. And there is no need for me to drive the nail in
my hand; I can do it because I know that hammers are used for that
purpose. But if, instead of being aware of the nail, I am simply aware
of the hammer, then all the difficulties begin. It is obvious that if
I am aware of the hammer I may drive the nail in my hand. I may even
drive it in the wrong place. But I cannot drive it at all. If I am aware
of the nail I may drive the hammer into my hand; but I can certainly do
so far more easily than I could drive the nail.
